subject: Civil Engineering
title: Pavement Design Methods
description: A micro-lesson that makes Pavement Design Methods usable.

hook.text: How thick should a road be? Too thin and it cracks. Too thick and you waste millions.

buildup.text: AASHTO's empirical method uses the 1960s road test — results from real pavement sections.

discovery.text: Mechanistic-empirical design models stress and strain in each layer — physics-based.

twist.text: One heavy truck does the damage of 10,000 cars. Truck traffic drives pavement thickness.

climax.text: ESALs convert all traffic to equivalent 18,000-pound axle loads — the universal metric.

punchline.text: Pavement thickness is really about counting trucks, not cars.

quiz.question: Why do trucks dominate pavement design calculations?
options: Trucks travel faster and cause more surface friction
One heavy truck causes damage equivalent to thousands of car passes
Trucks use different lanes than cars, concentrating damage

details.summary: Pavement design methods determine required layer thicknesses based on expected traffic loads, subgrade strength, climate, and material properties. The AASHTO empirical method uses serviceability equations from road test data.
details.whyItMatters: Under-designed pavements fail prematurely, costing agencies millions in repairs. Over-designed pavements waste materials and money. Accurate design methods optimize performance per dollar spent over the pavement's life.
takeaways: Traffic is converted to equivalent single axle loads for standardized design
Subgrade strength measured by resilient modulus or CBR determines required thickness
Mechanistic-empirical methods predict specific distress types like fatigue cracking

faq.question: What is an equivalent single axle load and why is it used?
faq.answer: An ESAL converts all axle types and weights to the damage equivalent of one standard 80-kN axle. A fully loaded truck can equal thousands of ESALs because pavement damage increases exponentially with axle weight. This converts mixed traffic into a single design parameter.

faq.question: How does the mechanistic-empirical approach improve pavement design?
faq.answer: It calculates actual stresses and strains within each pavement layer using material properties and traffic loads, then predicts specific distress types through damage models. This approach accounts for local climate, materials, and traffic patterns better than purely empirical methods.
